items.title: A broken thermometer at a Chattanooga school resulted in a hazmat response and multiple people being transported to the...
items.content_text:
A broken thermometer at a Chattanooga school resulted in a hazmat response and multiple people being transported to the hospital Wednesday morning. On 9/23/26, Blue Shift companies responded to Dalewood Middle School at 1300 Shallowford Road after students and teachers were possibly exposed to mercury. 
 A thermometer was dropped during a routine experiment in a science lab. At first, it was suspected of containing mercury. It has now been determined that the thermometer was alcohol based and there was no harm to students or staff. 
 Officials treated the incident as a possible mercury exposure until the substance could be identified by an environmental company. 
 Fourteen students were transported by ambulance or personal vehicle to the hospital. Two teachers were also transported. They were taken to the hospital as a precautionary measure.
 The heating and air conditioning was shut down to the building and the rest of the student body was dismissed.
 Marion Environmental responded to the school to handle the remediation and confirmed that it was an alcohol thermometer. No mercury was involved. 
 CFD Hazmat 1, Special Operations, Squad 1, Engine 15, and members of the command staff responded to Dalewood Middle, in addition to CPD, Hamilton County EMS and officials with Hamilton County Schools.

A strong region is built when communities have the resources, partnerships and capacity to move forward together.

Today, we’re proud to share the Southeast Tennessee Development District 2026 Annual Report, reflecting a year of meaningful investment and collaboration across the communities we serve.

This year, SETD helped secure $51.9 million in grant funding for local governments, managed more than $450 million in community projects, connected thousands of older adults and individuals with disabilities with critical resources, and provided 13,433 workforce services to 721 regional employers.

But the story of this year is bigger than any one number.

It can be seen in infrastructure moving from plans to reality, new investments reaching our communities, people gaining skills and pathways to employment, older adults remaining connected and independent, and local leaders working across community lines to address shared priorities.

That is the role SETD is proud to play: bringing people, resources and expertise together to help Southeast Tennessee turn shared goals into progress.

None of this work happens alone. We are grateful to our local governments, board members, funding partners, community organizations and regional partners who continue to trust us and work alongside us.

Building Together for a Thriving Southeast Tennessee.

 Strickler, an associate professor of political science and UTC faculty member since 2016, used his fall 2025 leave to advance research on presidential leadership and U.S. drug control policy, co-author a book chapter about camping, and develop a new course on American political culture.
 The projects look different on paper, but each grew from questions that have long shaped his teaching and research: how institutions influence public life, how people make meaning together and how ideas become action.

Commission Meeting Summary — September 21, 2026
 Airport Advisory Board: The commission approved Resolution 583, formally appointing Jack Farrow, John Record, Heath Merz, Michael Brown, and Zoe Krohne to the Airport Advisory Board.
 Airport Retaining Wall: The commission approved a $55,000 task order with Ardurra Group (parent company of Cannon & Cannon) to design repairs for the failing retaining wall behind the Airport Terminal, funded through the enterprise fund. Commissioners discussed drainage concerns, road conditions, and financing options, and agreed to get a rough budget after preliminary design before finalizing how the project will be paid for.
 Also approved: FY27 Airport Maintenance Grant Contract and the August Finance Report.
 City Manager's Report:
 - The city will take over direct management of the library, ending its contract with the outside provider, and will coordinate with the state regional library system for ordinance updates & guidance.
 - Imagination Station: Cannon & Cannon is developing proposals; a public open house is being proposed so residents can review and ask questions.
 - Iron Rail Cams will propose live-view cameras at the Thatcher Switch/Tucker Road railroad crossing — at no cost to the city.
 - A new commissioner orientation book is in the works, along with Sunshine Law training for city boards.
 Commissioner Remarks:
 - The city's audit is underway, with a first draft expected around October.
 - A citizen-suggested idea for a library food pantry will be discussed at an upcoming workshop.
 - Christmas Parade Survey results will be presented at the commission workshop on Monday, September 28th.
 Watch the full meeting recording here: https://www.collegedaletn.gov/…/agenda…/livestream/index.php

items.content_text:
Condé Nast Traveler has named Chattanooga one of 25 Bright Ideas in Travel 2026 honorees worldwide.  
 We're featured alongside organizations and countries like American Airlines, Air New Zealand, Etihad Rail, UNESCO, and Greenland.
 The list's accompanying feature on Chattanooga as North America’s first National Park City puts our community’s people and partnerships in the spotlight:
 • Gail Loveland Barille at Outdoor Chattanooga
 • Linda Mines, Chattanooga-Hamilton County historian
 • Laura Marsh at Chattanooga Audubon Society
 • The conservation scientists and Alison Pryor at the Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute
 • Will O'Hearn at the Chattanooga-Hamilton County Bicentennial Public Library
 • Mayor Tim Kelly with the City of Chattanooga
 • Chattanooga Riverboat Company and Chattanooga Audubon Society, whose Maclellan Island Eco Tours partnership opens the story
 Over three days here, reporter Daliah Singer connected with people who know this region deeply and could explain the work already underway. More than 5,600 residents signed the National Park City charter, and the Seeds program helped turn that commitment into projects.
 That’s what gives a destination’s story substance: knowledgeable people, meaningful partnerships, and work a journalist can see firsthand.
 To everyone who shared their expertise: thank you for helping tell Chattanooga’s story.
 Who should the next visiting journalist meet? If your organization has someone with expertise in conservation, history, outdoor access, food, music, or the built environment, let Chattanooga Tourism Co. know. Help us connect the next reporter with the people doing the work.

items.content_text:
Meet the Emerging Producer! 
 Tim Moore is an independent small-business marketer based in Chattanooga, where he’s lived since 2015. He specializes in working with restaurants, hospitality brands, and brick-and-mortar businesses, helping them grow, tell clearer stories, and connect with their communities. His passion for food and storytelling also led him to create Tim Eats, an online channel highlighting local food and the chefs, owners, and teams behind it all—featuring not just what’s on the plate, but the humans who make it happen. 
 This Saturday, September 26, Tim will partner with local business Good Kinsmen for Beyond the Plate, a free culinary experience where Chattanooga chefs will highlight the stories, techniques, and cultural influences behind their food.
 "Beyond the Plate is about closing the distance between the people who cook and the people who eat," said Tim Moore, founder of Tim Eats. "I wanted to build something free and open, where anyone in Chattanooga can walk in and connect with the chefs shaping our food scene, and hopefully learn something they can bring home to their own kitchens."
 Learn more and RSVP at https://tim-eats.com/beyond-the-plate 
 📍 Good Kinsmen
 📅 September 26, 12-6 PM

CPD Investigating Deadly Crash Involving a Pedestrian on Shallowford Road
 CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is investigating a crash that resulted in a pedestrian's death Monday afternoon.
 At approximately 11:00 a.m., CPD's Traffic Unit responded to a crash involving a pedestrian in the 7500 block of Shallowford Road. Preliminary findings indicate the pedestrian, a 65-year-old woman, was attempting to cross the road and stepped in front of a vehicle. The driver attempted to swerve, but still hit the pedestrian.
 Hamilton County EMS responded and transported the woman to the hospital where she was pronounced dead. 
 This information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. Chattanooga Police ask anyone with information regarding this incident to call 423-698-2525.
 #CPDnews

items.title: Before you decide mountain biking "isn't for you," we need to clear a few things up. 👀🚲 You do NOT need your own mount...
items.content_text:
Before you decide mountain biking "isn't for you," we need to clear a few things up. 👀🚲
 You do NOT need your own mountain bike.
 You do NOT need experience.
 You do NOT need to show up ready to ride singletrack.
 You don't even need to know what half the parts of a mountain bike are called.
 That's what Trail Quest is for.
 Field FUNdamentals starts with the basics in a controlled environment at Greenway Farm, where you can practice things like braking, shifting, balance, body position and bike control before ever taking those skills onto a trail.
 Bike and helmet reservations are available, classes are just $10, and beginners are very much invited.
 All you really need is a pair of closed-toed shoes and a willingness to try something new.
 🗓Tuesdays through November 3
 📍Greenway Farm
 🎟Register at outdoorchattanooga.com/calendar
 Come see what all the mountain biking hype is about!
